articles.title: IFRC: One month after Venezuela's earthquakes, health care, psychosocial support and safe water remain urgent priorities
articles.description: Country: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Caracas, Panama City, Geneva 23 July 2026 — One month after the two earthquakes that struck north-central Venezuela, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and the Venezuelan Red Cross (VRC) have identified three critical areas for humanitarian assistance in the short and medium term: primary health care, mental health care and access to safe drinking water. The IFRC and the VRC are now focusing their efforts on distributing humanitarian aid, delivering health services and carrying out further needs assessments. Their findings show that many families still depend on bottled water to drink, wash and cook. Access to sanitation also remains limited, raising the risk of disease outbreaks in the areas where displaced people are staying. Thousands of people with chronic conditions have yet to fully regain continuity of treatment — an interruption that threatens their wellbeing and can add further strain to the health system. Survivors are also living with anxiety, fear, sadness and sleeplessness as they grieve the loss of loved ones, of their jobs and of their livelihoods. "One month on from the devastating earthquakes that shook our country, we reaffirm our commitment to the Venezuelan people. We have activated every cooperation mechanism of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement to strengthen and complement our response, and we will remain here for those who need it most," said Luis Manuel Farías Villanueva, President of the Venezuelan Red Cross. "We are planning a 24-month operation to keep standing with people; needs have been changing, and our response has adjusted to serve more people and to serve them better." From the very first minute, local Red Cross teams have been alongside the people affected: first setting up a field hospital, supporting the rescue of survivors and reconnecting families who had lost track of their loved ones; and now, distributing humanitarian aid and strengthening primary health care through an emergency clinic in La Guaira. The clinic, set up by the IFRC and managed by the Spanish Red Cross, reinforces the Venezuelan Red Cross field hospital. It will operate for four months and is already delivering health and psychosocial services that will benefit close to 30,000 people. One of them is Gabriel Cipriani, who lost close relatives when his building collapsed and lives with a neurological condition that requires constant medication. For him, the Red Cross remaining there is the difference between continuing his treatment and having it interrupted: "Knowing I can count on a Red Cross doctor made me feel that I am not alone, that there is a hand with me. That gives you security, it gives you confidence." In the coming weeks and months, the priority for the IFRC and the VRC will be to sustain that health care and expand access to safe water while laying the foundations for recovery: strengthening epidemiological surveillance to prevent outbreaks, maintaining psychosocial support and treatment for chronic conditions, and beginning to accompany families as they rebuild their livelihoods. Assistance will be adjusted as needs change, with particular attention to those at greatest risk: children, older people, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and people with chronic illnesses or disabilities. "This disaster is far from over. Continuing to distribute essential items and safeguarding people's wellbeing and public health is, and will remain, a priority in the medium term — but further ahead it will also mean making sure people recover their livelihoods and their income-generating activities," said Loyce Pace, IFRC Regional Director for the Americas*. "A disaster like this one calls for assistance that is multisectoral, comprehensive and sustained over time. The IFRC is committed to the Venezuelan Red Cross and to the people of Venezuela in making that possible — and that is why we are calling for sustained, flexible funding, able to accompany families throughout their recovery."* That funding has a concrete figure. The IFRC launched an Emergency Appeal to raise 50 million Swiss francs to assist 300,000 people over two years. One month on from the disaster, it is 25.19 per cent funded. As people's needs evolve and grow more complex, the resources to meet them should grow at the same pace. Johannes Chinchilla, +584 222 550278 Susana Arroyo Barrantes, +507 6999-3199 Tommaso Della Longa +41 (0) 79 708 4367 | Scott Craig +41 (0) 79 76 370 3575

Moon Alert

Caution! Avoid shopping (except food and gas) or making important decisions all day until 8:30 p.m. After that, the moon moves from Scorpio into Sagittarius.

Aries (March 21-April 19)

A positive day

Today, Mercury stops being retrograde, which will help you get more organized at home. Nevertheless, opportunities for vacations, sports events and fun socializing with others continue to come your way. At work, co-workers are supportive. It’s all good.

Taurus (April 20-May 20)

A positive day

Be aware of the limitations of the moon alert today and agree to nothing important. Meanwhile, good news! Today Mercury stops being retrograde, which will reduce transportation delays, car problems and mixed-up communications that you've been dealing with for a while. Brighter skies ahead!

Gemini (May 21-June 20)

An average day

With fiery Mars in your sign now, you have a lot of energy and drive. However, be aware of the limitations of today's moon alert. (See above.) You'll be happy to know that Mercury stops being retrograde today, which will improve your finances, especially in terms of delays and mistakes.

Cancer (June 21-July 22)

A positive day

Excellent news! Mercury has been retrograding in your sign since June 29. Today this is over, which means your life will resume a greater degree of normalcy, and silly mistakes will be reduced along with delays and transportation problems. Thank goodness!

Leo (July 23-Aug. 22)

A positive day

Be aware of today's moon alert. Fortunately, you are in a strong position because both the sun and lucky Jupiter are in your sign. Fiery Mars is also well-placed, promoting teamwork, competitive sports and athletics. Starting today, life takes on a forward momentum.

Virgo (Aug. 23-Sept. 22)

A positive day

With Venus in your sign, you're enjoying socializing with others. Nevertheless, you also have a strong tendency now to work alone or behind the scenes. You're also ambitious to achieve. With this in mind, be aware that there is a moon alert today. Volunteer for nothing.

Libra (Sept. 23-Oct. 22)

An average day

For the last month, Mercury has been retrograding at the top of your chart, affecting your relations with bosses, parents and authority figures from the past. As of today, this is over. Although you might be focused on financial matters, restrict spending to food and gas.

Scorpio (Oct. 23-Nov. 21)

A positive day

Today the moon is in your sign, which gives you a slight advantage over the other signs. However, most of this day is a moon alert! (See above.) Therefore, tread carefully and restrict your spending to food and gas. Don't volunteer for anything. Postpone important decisions.

Sagittarius (Nov. 22-Dec. 21)

An average day

It's encouraging that Mercury retrograde is over today because it might have delayed financial matters for you, especially dealing with third parties, partners or the government. Go forward with confidence now to make plans for travel, publishing, medicine, the law and higher education. (Whew!)

Capricorn (Dec. 22-Jan. 19)

A positive day

In the last month, Mercury has been retrograding opposite your sign, attracting ex-partners and old friends back into your world. (This might have been a mixed blessing for some.) At any rate, as of today, Mercury retrograde is finished. However, check the Moon Alert above!

Aquarius (Jan. 20-Feb. 18)

A positive day

You'll be relieved to know that today Mercury retrograde stops, as it has been creating equipment problems, delays, and confusion with respect to your job, your health, and even perhaps dealing with your pet. This means your efforts to work will be more efficient and reliable. Yay! (Check moon alert.)

Pisces (Feb. 19-March 20)

An average day

Today you might feel restless for adventure or a change. You're working hard, but you also want to explore something new. Fortunately, Mercury stops being retrograde today. Nevertheless, most of this day is a moon alert, so just bide your time. It's all systems go tomorrow!

If today is your birthday

Actor Daniel Radcliffe (1989) shares your birthday today. You are fun-loving, likable and helpful. People respond to your optimism and easygoing manner. This is a year of work and construction. Build foundations in your life, both externally and internally. Simplicity is key. Take charge of your health. Explore martial arts or yoga. Stay grounded and levelheaded.

articles.title: Besieged by lobbyists, will UK ministers protect our ecosystems? No, they’ll chicken out | George Monbiot
articles.description: Industrial poultry farming is killing our rivers. But rather than stop it, the government has been facilitating it. Will Andy Burnham end this ecocide? There’s a slightly mean question I often ask British people with an interest in the living world: can you name the environment secretary? I don’t intend to show them up: it’s not them I’m testing. I watch the brows knit, a finger go up, the mouth open and close. “It’s, you know, the one who ... no, they went, didn’t they? That other one ...” It’s been like this for seven years. Why? Because throughout this period, we’ve not had environment secretaries. We’ve had portals through which corporate lobbyists may pass. The last incumbent to represent the wider public interest (and I can scarcely bring myself to type these words) was Michael Gove. In his other roles, he’s widely remembered with loathing and disgust. Out of office, he continues to poison public life , as editor of the Spectator. But in this role, to general astonishment, he placed the public good above special interests. George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: DZA: Fire - 07-2026 - Algeria: Wildfires – July 2026 (2026-07-22)
articles.description: Country: Algeria Sources: Croissant-Rouge Algérien, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. Description On 18 July 2026, the wildfire emergency in Algeria reached a significant operational peak, with 154 forest, vegetation and agricultural fires recorded within 24 hours across several wilayas. Of these, 138 fires were extinguished, while 16 remained active at the time of reporting. The fires affected northern, north-eastern, central and western Algeria, including Annaba, Souk Ahras, Skikda, Guelma, Bouira, Médéa, Mila, Mascara, El Tarf, Jijel, Sétif, Béjaïa, Tlemcen, Saïda, Tissemsilt, Biskra and Chlef. Over the last 24 hours, the Ministry of the Interior, Local Authorities and Transport confirmed six fatalities linked to the wildfires. In Seraïdi, Annaba, more than 100 patients were evacuated from a rehabilitation hospital, while approximately 150 homes were affected or threatened. Preventive evacuations were also carried out in several localities, including El Tarf, Béjaïa, Guelma and Bouira. The Government of Algeria has led a strong and coordinated national response, ensuring the rapid mobilization of the competent authorities and emergency services. Efforts have focused on protecting lives, supporting affected communities, securing threatened areas and maintaining close operational coordination across the affected wilayas. The Algerian Red Crescent mobilized its provinces committees, volunteers and logistical resources from the beginning of the emergency. Teams provided first aid, drinking water, food assistance, psychosocial support and essential humanitarian assistance to affected communities and emergency responders. Response and monitoring activities continue, while high temperatures, dry vegetation, difficult terrain and the risk of fire re-ignition remain important operational considerations. Request For Assistance Government Requests International Assistance: No NS Requests International Assistance: Yes Information Bulletin Published No Actions taken by National Society General Water & Sanitation First Aid Health Evacuation Shelter Search & Rescue Food aid Psychosocial support services Summary Actions taken by others The Algerian Red Crescent mobilized its wilaya committees, National Response Teams (NRT), trained first aiders, volunteers and logistical resources from the beginning of the emergency. Teams provided first aid, supported evacuations, distributed drinking water, meals and relief items, conducted rapid needs assessments, and offered psychosocial support to affected families and frontline responders in coordination with local authorities and Civil Protection. Planned International Response DREF: Planned

articles.title: Venezuela | Earthquake - Operation Update #1 (MDRVE015)
articles.description: Country: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. A. SITUATION ANALYSIS Description of the crisis On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with preliminary magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5. Authorities have reported more than 1,000 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity. The event occurred during the San Juan festivities, a national celebration that attracts large numbers of people to coastal areas; and as many workplaces were closed, this also led to families having many or all members present inside their home when the earthquakes happened. In La Guaira, a popular destination to spend this festivity, this resulted in higher population concentrations in public spaces and along the coastline at the time of the event, increasing the number of people potentially exposed to the impacts of the earthquakes. As of 15 July, 4,829 people were reported dead, 16,740 injured and approximately 17,907 had lost their homes due to severe damage to housing1. It is expected for these figures to continue to rise in coming days as the Search and Rescue phase focused on extraction of survivors moves towards a focus on recovery, identification and return to family members of bodies retrieved from collapsed structures. Response teams from over 29 countries deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG)2. International search and rescue deployments are progressively concluding, with several Movement teams having completed their missions. A response focused on search, recovery, debris-removal, shelter provision and efforts to bridge emergency relief to recovery and reconstruction efforts continues under national leadership, with a broad range of bilateral and multilateral support focused on humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery. According to OCHA, 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some degree of damage, with 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.3 A comprehensive technical evaluation of structures is underway by respective authorities to identify homes that can be repaired and those that are too dangerous to return to. Evaluation of safe areas to build permanent housing for those affected is also taking place. Damage to residences, commercial buildings and critical infrastructure also disrupted the functioning of electricity, water-supply, telecommunications and transport systems, as well as public transportation and airport operations. Damaged roads and bridges have also restricted access and affected movement to and within some affected areas. The healthcare capacity has been particularly affected, with limited supply of water systems. More than 400 schools were also reported as affected, while some have been repurposed as temporary shelters until the academic cycle resumes after the summer. Damage to water systems has further affected the availability of basic services. Moreover, it is important to note that the main affected area, La Guaira, fulfils multiple critical functions for the country. Its proximity to the Capital, Caracas, the presence of the country’s main international airport (Maiquetía) and one of its major ports, makes it a strategic transportation, logistics, trade, tourism, fishing and service hub. Consequently, the incident impacted not only local communities and visitors present, but also essential infrastructure and activities that facilitate connectivity and the supply of goods to the capital and other regions of the country. This increases the number of people and logistical capacity affected. The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with thousands of injured, many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, and with families displaced after the destruction or severe damage of their homes. Beyond these physical impacts, the earthquakes have also had significant effects on the mental health and psychosocial well-being of affected people. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, uncertainty regarding housing and recovery, and exposure to damaged environments and recovery operations has contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected populations. Notably, La Guaira’s geographical location is prone to various types of emergencies. In December 1999, torrential rainfall triggered catastrophic landslides, flash floods and debris flows across the then State of Vargas—now La Guaira—causing widespread destruction and displacement. The exact death toll remains uncertain; however, the United States Geological Survey estimated that between 15,000 and 30,000 people were killed. The current earthquake has therefore affected communities with lived and intergenerational memories of one of Venezuela’s most severe disasters.
